summary: A feature piece on the Weeping Stone, a slab of rock at the edge of Aelfwood forest near the village of Glenharrow, and the curse legend around it. The author gathers accounts from a descendant of the legend's central figure, a tavern regular, a historian, a psychic medium, geologists and a B&B owner. The legend, a mix of folklore, coincidence and tourism, is shown to be a lasting part of the community's identity, though no empirical evidence explains the weeping.
one_line: Interviews with Glenharrow locals, a historian and a medium explore the legend of the cursed Weeping Stone and its place in village identity.
key_facts: The Weeping Stone is an irregular slab of ancient rock on the edge of the Aelfwood forest near the village of Glenharrow.
Legend says touching the stone under moonlight ensnares a person in a curse that brings misfortune on themselves and their loved ones.
Elspeth McAllister, a descendant of Adaira McAllister, told the origin tale on September 5, 2023.
In the winter of 1784, Adaira McAllister was betrothed to soldier Ewan Macrae, who went to war and sent no word; she waited and wept by the stone, then was found dead at its base.
Villagers buried Adaira with the stone marking her grave, and days later the stone began to weep water, which continues irregularly today.
Finley Doyle, at Ye Olde Tavern on September 13, 2023, said his great-uncle Alistair touched the stone under a waning moon in autumn 1946 while mocking the curse.
Within a fortnight of touching the stone, Alistair lost his farm animals to an unexplained illness, his wife fell into deep melancholy, and the land never yielded as before.

Dr. Ian Campbell, a local historian, said on September 22, 2023 that stones weeping can be a natural environmental reaction, that an Adaira McAllister did live and supposedly die there, and that records show spikes in misfortune around when Alistair allegedly touched the stone.

Psychic medium Rowena Halbrook said that she and three others held a séance at the stone and that it wept 'as if in anguish'; the encounter was on October 2, 2023 under a harvest moon, and no empirical evidence was found.
A team of geologists from the University of Edinburgh came last summer to analyze the stone's composition and the source of the weeping, but results were inconclusive.
Nora Fleming, owner of a bed and breakfast near the forest, says the legend is good for business but attracts thrill-seekers who lack respect for local traditions.
Glenharrow has seen a steady rise in visitors in recent years because of the stone.
